      <title>Third Ebola case in Kenya highlights US failures amid Trump cuts to key services</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/19/ebola-cases-kenya-us-quarantine</link>
      <description><p>Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO</p><p>A third person in Kenya has tested positive for Bundibugyo ebolavirus in the country’s first-ever cluster of Ebola cases, as the second-largest outbreak in history kills more than 4,300 and sickens more than 9,000 people in the region.</p><p>It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/19/ebola-cases-kenya-us-quarantine">Continue reading...</a></description>

News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:58:45 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>Perspective</category><title>France 'has to assist' Gulf states, diplomat says as Macron makes three-day visit</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/perspective/20261019-france-has-to-assist-gulf-states-diplomat-says-as-macron-makes-three-day-visit</link><description>
French President Emmanuel Macron is making a three-day visit to the Gulf states focused on fuel supplies and strategic ties. The French leader will first visit Kuwait before heading to the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar. The Elysée Palace said Macron would seek commitments for additional deliveries of diesel and petrol that could increase supplies available to France.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/18f90ec2-cbb8-11f1-aa50-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-7a120f6d.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/18f90ec2-cbb8-11f1-aa50-2d1c143cdef3/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-7a120f6d.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">4b189c3c-cb9b-11f1-bda7-1988d4dc9461</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:43:41 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Oliver FARRY</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Italy hit by violent cost-of-living protests, mostly minors arrested</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261019-italy-hit-by-violent-cost-of-living-protests-mostly-minors-arrested</link><description>
Youths and police clashed for a second consecutive day on Sunday in Milan, where at least 200 people were arrested during protests over the cost of living. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called a security meeting for Monday to address the violence, which evoked scenes of chaos and looting in Paris. FRANCE 24's Seema Gupta reports from Rome, Italy. 
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/9e105c50-ca6e-11f1-8f14-4dd8ac2cf3bf/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26290687058313.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/9e105c50-ca6e-11f1-8f14-4dd8ac2cf3bf/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26290687058313.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">700beb90-cba8-11f1-ad30-132606c66d67</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:30:39 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>REPLAY: French PM speaks after crisis meeting</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261019-replay-french-pm-speaks-after-crisis-meeting</link><description>
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Monday said he had asked regional authorities to impose curfews in some cities. The measures, which he said would be "partial" and "localised", are intended to protect businesses after weekend demonstrations spilled over into street violence. Lecornu also accused the "ultra-left movement" of seeking to "orchestrate deep unrest across the country" in the runup to next year's presidential election. Watch our replay.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/31ca19d2-cbb3-11f1-8769-6313a763b466/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261019-122904-124834-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/31ca19d2-cbb3-11f1-8769-6313a763b466/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261019-122904-124834-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">399fb78e-cbb3-11f1-b804-1dd46b1fcbed</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:21:24 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Focus</category><title>Inflation squeezes households as Lebanon's economic crisis persists</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/focus/20261019-inflation-squeezes-households-as-lebanon-s-economic-crisis-persists</link><description>
Lebanon's economic crisis has dragged on since 2019. A re-igniting of Israel's war with Hezbollah derailed the weak recovery seen last year. The World Bank now forecasts that the Lebanese economy will shrink by 6.4 percent this year, with inflation expected to reach around 17.5 percent. A growing divide is visible everywhere: in households, in businesses and even in consumer habits. Our correspondents Serge Berberi and Renée Davis report.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/a41d5f50-cba7-11f1-9113-d1d2c32ebb87/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-a644ee1b.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/a41d5f50-cba7-11f1-9113-d1d2c32ebb87/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-a644ee1b.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">5a73357e-c976-11f1-b135-e1f288cffd1d</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:18:17 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Serge BERBERI</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Les Misérables: Macron's 'sense of detachment' amid rising living costs and youth 'fears for future'</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261019-les-mis%C3%A9rables-macron-s-sense-of-detachment-amid-rising-living-costs-youth-fears-for-the-future</link><description>
France’s escalating protest movement is exposing a widening disconnect between political leadership and public frustration, while raising questions about the country’s long tradition of social unrest. Chris Reynolds, Professor of French and European Studies at Nottingham Trent University, argues that President Emmanuel Macron’s latest address was characterised by a troubling “sense of detachment,” offering little to resolve the structural grievances driving the demonstrations. Drawing parallels with May 1968 and the Yellow Vest movement, Reynolds warns that violent unrest risks eclipsing the legitimate concerns of largely peaceful protesters, undermining public sympathy and reshaping political debate ahead of the presidential election. 
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/f36e6188-cba4-11f1-ad70-4dd8ac2cf3bf/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261019-080654-081709-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/f36e6188-cba4-11f1-ad70-4dd8ac2cf3bf/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261019-080654-081709-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">f976f270-cba4-11f1-9199-47f36f8ab248</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 11:00:19 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ Did a giant object collide with Earth to form the moon? ]]> For as long as humans have watched the night sky, we have wondered about the moon, pondering everything from its alien appearance to its influence over phenomena on Earth such as ocean tides, climate stability, and even the natural rhythms of many organisms.

Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins, and how long has it orbited Earth?

Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours. Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia. The material ejected into orbit by the powerful impact in question would have accumulated afterward, forming the moon that we observe today.

What do we know?

Birth of a lunar origin hypothesis

The evolution of this striking solution to one of the moon's most enduring mysteries goes back to 1946, when geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly was among the first to suggest that an impact event might explain the formation of the moon.

Before Daly, scientists had been leaning toward theories that involved Earth's rapid spin billions of years ago, when each day may have at one time lasted as little as 2 or 3 hours. Decades later in the 1970s, researchers William Hartmann and Donald Davis developed their own models involving collisions of large bodies left over from planetary formation, which could collide with younger planets.

Building on such ideas, other researchers went on to propose similar scenarios between the early Earth and a Mars-sized object. Early in the following decade, the concept eventually claimed its place as the leading lunar-formation process during a landmark conference held in Kona, Hawaii, in 1984.

Evidence of a planetary-scale collision

The popularity of the giant-impact hypothesis can be attributed to the multiple lines of evidence supporting the impact scenario. For instance, researchers have long recognized the similar stable-isotope ratios between both moon rocks and those from Earth, strongly suggesting a link between their origins.

Additionally, the unusually high angular momentum (or spin) of the Earth-moon system, when compared to observations of other rocky planets, also could be explained as one of the effects of a massive collision.

Further clues can be found in the moon's composition, which reveals a relatively small iron core and lower density. This is significant to astronomers, since a hypothetical giant impact would have seen the suspected Theia protoplanet's metallic core merging with the young Earth's interior — meanwhile, lighter mantle and crust material from both worlds would have become dislodged and blasted into orbit, eventually helping form the moon.

Another important piece of evidence involves the relative depletion of volatile substances (a chemical that easily turns into gas or vapor at room temperatures) in lunar material, which again suggests that it might have been lost during an extremely energetic event, an idea further supported by evidence that the early moon once possessed a substantial magma ocean.

What remains unknown?

New research expands on the Theia hypothesis

Still, several significant questions remain, including what precise conditions led to the impact, and how the resulting planetary material evolved into the moon as it appears today.

Recently, a new study by Adeene Denton of Southwest Research Institute and colleagues at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory put a new spin on the Theia hypothesis, suggesting that the suspected ancient impact may have been significantly influenced by the heat and physical strength of the two colliding bodies.

The team's findings challenge some long-held views about the giant-impact hypothesis, while lending new support to others. For instance, the team's simulations revealed that while some impacts lead to the creation of a disk of debris that later coalesces into a moon, under other conditions, simulations support the idea that the moon could have been formed in a remarkably short period of time — perhaps within around five hours.

However, one of the primary issues with determining the exact conditions of the giant-impact hypothesis involves the ongoing debate over the moon's age.

"There is a large controversy regarding the age of the moon," said Dr. Erik Asphaug, a planetary science professor at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and one of the new study's co-authors.

In an email to Space, Asphaug explained some of the issues arising from this, since current estimates place the timing of the moon's formation anywhere from around 40 to 120 million years after the formation of the solar system. Therein lies part of the issue, according to Asphaug, who says this timing could have significant implications for models of the Theia impact.

If it had been an earlier collision, Asphaug says this would have involved a hotter Theia due to the greater degree of radiogenic heating; by contrast, a later impact would have meant a cooler and stronger Theia.

"I don't think we know enough yet to say the moon (and by corollary, the Earth) formed this way or that way," Asphaug told Space. "But knowing how temperature affects the result opens up a new dimension for viewing the problem, and that is always helpful because it shifts our frame of reference, like getting out of the car to have a walk around."

A lunar enigma in time and space

For researchers like Asphaug, understanding the moon's formation requires looking at it as more than just an event in space, but also as one in time. Doing so allows comparisons between three different metrics: isotopic decay, temperature-dependent material strength, and the geological record of debris striking other planets — a process through which he believes tighter constraints could be placed on precisely when the moon-forming impact might have occurred.

Adeene Denton, the study's lead author, also emphasized the introduction of the time component her team's research brings to the table, telling Space in an email that the outcome of the moon-forming impact could have depended significantly on the timing of the collision.

"Before, scientists have generally assumed that the outcome of the collision will be the same regardless of when it takes place," Denton wrote. "But now we know that temperature's effect on material properties, which is dictated by how old and/or cold the proto-Earth and Theia might be, alters things substantially."

By connecting impact simulations to data related to the moon's geochemical record, as well as models of early solar system formation, Denton thinks her team's work could help scientists better constrain precisely how and when the moon formed.

The mystery continues

For now, in terms of which possible scenario — an earlier or later collision event — emerges as being the most likely, Denton says it's still difficult to say.

"It depends on which scenarios for solar system formation you favor," Denton told Space.

"I am generally in favor of an earlier formation of the moon, consistent with a rapid planet-building phase in our solar system," Denton said, "but we can't neglect the possibility that the moon formed late."

While much work remains to be done, Denton and Asphaug believe their findings help significantly advance present efforts to resolve some of the questions about the giant-impact hypothesis — a few of which have lingered now for many years.

For Asphaug, however, such lingering questions may simply be part of the scientific process.

"Science has a way of wandering around for a long time until finally it all comes to focus," Asphaug said.

"I believe that will happen, in part thanks to this work, in the coming decade."

]]> <![CDATA[ Japan launching bold sample-return mission to Mars moon Phobos today: Watch it live ]]>

Japan will launch an epic mission to Mars today (Oct. 19), and you can watch the action live.

The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is scheduled to lift off atop an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 local Japan time).

You can watch it live via the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Coverage will begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT).

As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars' two moons, Phobos and Deimos. They're both tiny compared to Earth's own moon; Phobos is just 14 miles (22 kilometers) wide, and Deimos is even smaller, with a diameter of about 8 miles (13 km).

They're also quite mysterious. While astronomers have a pretty clear understanding of our own moon's birth — it coalesced from material blasted into space when a Mars-sized planet slammed into Earth long ago — there's no consensus about Phobos and Deimos' origin story.

The duo "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in an Oct. 15 statement. (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.)

"Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added.

]]> <![CDATA[ Astronomers want your help finding 'missing' black holes in the Milky Way ]]> Astronomers estimate that our home galaxy, the Milky Way, has churned out more than 10 million black holes over its 13-billion-year history. Yet so far, they have found only 70.

Now, a group of astronomers in the U.K. is trying to close that vast gap by enlisting the public. Their project, called Black Hole Hunters, is looking for volunteers with a computer and a few spare minutes to sift through troves of data gathered by a NASA space telescope. By flagging recognizable patterns that could point to a "missing" black hole, volunteers can help fast-track a search that would otherwise take years, the team says.

"You'll be narrowing down precisely where we need to point our telescopes next," project co-lead Adam McMaster, an astronomer at the University of Southampton in the U.K., said in a statement, "and you might be the one to discover a black hole."

Cosmic magnifying glasses

Black holes form when massive stars roughly 20 times heavier than our sun run out of fuel and collapse, leaving behind an abyss with gravity so immense that even light cannot escape. While invisible themselves, these cosmic behemoths reveal their presence by bending the light of nearby objects, and the Black Hole Hunters project is searching for one specific manifestation of this effect.

It happens thanks to the fact that massive stars often form in pairs, and a star can sometimes survive the violent supernova explosion that turns its companion into a black hole. When that happens, the two bodies continue to orbit each other. If such a duo aligns just right with Earth, the black hole will periodically pass directly between its companion star and our planet. And when it does, the black hole's gravity acts like a cosmic magnifying glass, bending and magnifying the star's light, causing it to briefly appear brighter to watchful telescopes.

To find these hidden giants, the project relies on data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, or TESS. Although the satellite's primary mission is to hunt for planets beyond our solar system, its method of data collection — tracking tiny, continuous changes in a star's brightness over time — is ideally suited for identifying black hole magnification events, the project description notes.

"It's a simple task with no expertise required," McMaster said in the statement. "We will show volunteers examples of what to look for so all they have to do is recognise the right patterns."

Automated algorithms conduct a preliminary sweep of the TESS data, screening millions of potential stars for the most obvious black hole candidate locations, according to the project description. But, the researchers say, artificial intelligence struggles with the messy realities of the cosmos, such as stellar flares and the natural pulsations of stars that can trick the algorithms into false positives.

The human touch

That makes human volunteers a key part of the search. To keep errors in check, each graph is shown to multiple volunteers, and their answers are combined so that individual mistakes average out, according to the project's website.

"I can search for black holes on my laptop from my bedroom — and could make a real impact on real space science," Grace Clarke, an undergraduate student of physics and astronomy at the University of Southampton who's involved with the project, said in the same statement. "The data's easy to understand — it's just pattern recognition — and you don't need a degree in astronomy to read it."

The crowdsourced shortlist of promising signals lets astronomers aim follow-up observations at specific stars, such as precise measurements of whether a star is being tugged at by an unseen companion. Those measurements take time and are expensive, so a good shortlist helps researchers spend scarce telescope time wisely, the team says.

Since launching on the Zooniverse platform in October 2021, the project has attracted nearly 23,000 volunteers, who have completed more than 12 million classifications, according to its website.

Before turning to TESS, the team ran a similar search using data from SuperWASP, a ground-based survey that, like TESS, monitored stars for signs of planets from 2004 to 2016. Those results are still being analyzed and are expected to be published soon.

The team also plans to widen its search with observations from other instruments, including the European Space Agency's Euclid mission and NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

"With potentially thousands of new discoveries, we need all the help we can get," McMaster said in the statement.

]]> <![CDATA[ 10 best places to see the 2027 total solar eclipse in Spain ]]> Spain is one of the easiest places in the world to experience the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027. Historical August cloud cover: 13%

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

Just 9 miles (14 km) across the Strait of Gibraltar from Morocco, the historic port town is known for its whitewashed old town, the medieval Castle of Guzmán el Bueno and its long, sandy beaches. On Oct. 17, 2016, Orbital ATK (now Northrop Grumman Space Systems) returned to flight, successfully launching a cargo shipment to the International Space Station (ISS) after its previous cargo mission failed to launch.

The private spaceflight company was contracted by NASA to fly cargo to the ISS, and stakes were high for this launch. Orbital ATK's last attempt nearly two years earlier ended in a catastrophic explosion a few seconds after liftoff.

Despite some delays, the newly upgraded Antares rocket flawlessly blasted off into the night sky from NASA's Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia. Six days later, the Cygnus cargo spacecraft arrived at the ISS to deliver food, supplies and science experiments to the crew.

Why it mattered

For the International Space Station to be able to sustain a continuous human occupancy, periodic cargo deliveries are needed. Russia fulfills part of this requirement with its Progress spacecraft, and both ESA (European Space Agency) and JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) have contributed with their Automated Transfer Vehicle (ATV) and H-II Transfer Vehicle (HTV), respectively.

For its part, NASA contracted with Orbital (today, Northrop Grumman) and SpaceX to fly commercial resupply service missions. Both were needed to keep the U.S. operating segment of the station well supplied and with the science and research materials needed for the crew's work.

Below is a video of the explosion

Though adjustments can be made to go without one or more of these vehicles for a short period of time, the Progress, Cygnus and Dragon are key components of the ISS's continuous operation. So returning a vehicle to flight after a catastrophic exploration is important to well-being of the International Space Station program.

As it happened, Antares would fly another 12 times before having to stand down again to be redesigned, but that is for a different This Day in Space entry.

]]> Víkend Křišťálového údolí 3 – Střední uměleckoprůmyslová škola sklářská (Kamenický Šenov 2026) https://www.vybezek.eu/295967-vikend-kristaloveho-udoli-3-stredni-umeleckoprumyslova-skola-sklarska-kamenicky-senov-2026/ Sun, 18 Oct 2026 18:36:05 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=295967 Víkend 17. a 18. října 2026 v Libereckém kraji opět ve znamení Křišťálového údolí, znovu se otevřely brány a dveře v mnoha sklárnách, ateliérech, výrobních provozech, muzeích a školách.

Když už ten Kamenický Šenov (Preciosa, muzeum), tak tedy i do třetice. Kdysi dávno jsem na nějakém dni otevřených dveří tady už byl, ale je to tak dávno, že jsem na webu v archivech nic pro srovnání nenašel. Pořád jsou tu dvě budovy naproti sobě přes ulici (i ta podzemní chodba tu prý stále je, ale už není běžně přístupná), nicméně přišel jsem si jako ve zcela jiném vesmíru. Několikapatrová moderní budova, kde je plno dílen, kabinetů, ateliérů a pracovišť, spousty exponátů po chodbách i v místnostech, zastřešené atrium se skleněnou lávkou. Připadalo mi, že ten dům nemá konce, že za každým schodištěm je ještě další patro, další chodby a další dveře. Studenti, pracující na všem možném, zdánlivě nemajícím se sklářstvím takřka nic společného – malba, kresba, mozaika, modelování z hlíny, linoryt, letování a pájení. A zakecal jsem se s jedním ze zdejších „zapálených“ pedagogů, držícího se dlouhé rodinné tradice, který naznačil další a další plány. Tož držím palce a myslím, že jsem tu nebyl naposled.

Těch míst je plno křížem krážem přes celý kraj. Už dlouho se opakovaně kochávám v Preciose, byl jsem kdysi také v Novém Boru v Crystalexu, a letos jsem si řekl, že nikam nespěchám a když už jsem jednou v Kamenickém Šenově, okouknu zas jednou místní muzeum. Rekonstrukce stále probíhá, takže funguje v minimalistickém režimu. Nicméně poseděl jsem, pokoukal a hlavně pokecal. A i o tom tenhle křišťálový víkend přece má být…

Je jedno, kolikrát už, prostě jsem opět vyrazil do Kamenického Šenova, protože tam to pokaždé stojí za podívání. A letos jsem se rozhodl nezůstat jen tam.

Trasa opět obměněná a ve dvou variantách, týmy organizátorů s úsměvem od parkoviště do nejzazších koutů areálu.

Prodej, soutěže, dílničky. Asi jediná velká změna, které jsem si všiml – letos si návštěvníci neměli možnost sami fouknout na huti. I tak musím znovu konstatovat – kdykoli zas!

Turnaje se zúčastnila čtyři chlapecká družstva, která mezi sebou poměřila své síly systémem každý s každým. Jednotlivá utkání se hrála na 15 minut.

Naši chlapci vstupovali do turnaje s jasným cílem, kterým bylo obhájit prvenství z loňského roku. Hned v úvodním utkání proti ZŠ Východní předvedli výborný výkon a zaslouženě zvítězili vysoko 8:0. Ve druhém zápase je čekalo družstvo Gymnázia Varnsdorf. Díky skvělému vstupu do utkání a zodpovědnému výkonu si naši hráči připsali další přesvědčivé vítězství, tentokrát 4:0. V posledním utkání se naši chlapci utkali s družstvem ZŠ Edisonova. Přestože si během zápasu vytvořili řadu slibných brankových příležitostí, jejich neproměňování přineslo dramatickou koncovku. Nakonec však dokázali těsné vedení udržet a po vítězství 3:2 mohli slavit zasloužený triumf.

Naši fotbalisté tak prošli celým turnajem bez ztráty jediného bodu, s celkovým skóre 15:2, a úspěšně obhájili loňské prvenství!

Celý turnaj proběhl v přátelské a sportovní atmosféře. Všechna zúčastněná družstva si zaslouží pochvalu za předvedené výkony a nasazení. Našim chlapcům děkujeme za vzornou reprezentaci školy. Podzimní hry však pokračují dál. Již 3. 11. 2026 se uskuteční další díl, ve kterém žáci poměří své síly v plavání. Už teď se těšíme!

Mgr. Patrik Klouda, ZŠ Varnsdorf, nám. E. Beneše
